channel.title: The Librarian's Ledger
channel.description: Writing on Bitcoin, money, and the people who regulate it — read from the filings and the footnotes — plus a standing board of the world's biggest assets, gold, silver, the largest companies and Bitcoin, ranked by what the market says they're worth.

item.title: One Send, Three Recipients, One Fee
item.description: Lightning in a Jar can now pay several people in a single on-chain send, silent-payment addresses included. The builder posted a test spend; I found it in the blockchain, checked the arithmetic, and looked for the matching change in the public repository. Here is what that one transaction shows, what batching does and doesn't buy you, and what I haven't tested.

item.title: One Dashboard, Fifty Accounts, No Human in the Loop
item.description: A video making the rounds on X shows a wall of phone screens, each one a social media account posting, replying and liking on its own — the poster's caption claims a single AI dashboard is orchestrating fifty of them at once. The clip is a provocation, not a product demo, but the real numbers behind "dead internet theory" don't need the video's help. Here's what's actually measured, what's just a claim, and what it means for anyone still scrolling in good faith.

item.title: The Bridge Loan Nobody Signed For
item.description: A ZeroHedge post making the rounds argues that $2-3 trillion a year of circular, on-and-off-balance-sheet AI financing is a bridge loan — one that only gets repaid once enterprise AI spend reaches about $3 trillion a year in 2031. I checked how real the "circular financing" part is and how solid the 2031 number actually looks.

item.title: The Vault Rule Got Rewritten the Day Before She Left
item.description: Today the SEC proposed the rule that decides whether your financial advisor can actually hold crypto for you, and it does something the custody rule hasn't done since it was written in response to Bernie Madoff: let the advisor be the vault. It also quietly blesses something the industry has been doing in a legal gray zone for years. The vote landed on commissioner Hester Peirce's second-to-last day on the job, and her own statement reads like a closing argument.

item.title: Two Lines Cross on the Page
item.description: A friend shared a tweet from Bitwise's CIO citing a San Francisco Fed chart on stablecoin issuers' growing Treasury holdings, with "the entire stablecoin ecosystem is going much, much higher." Another friend in the same group chat flagged the chart's scale. A third asked the more basic question: higher in what? I pulled the actual Fed letter to answer both.

item.title: The Committee That Won't Say Its Own Name
item.description: A policy paper published today calls index providers "Wall Street's invisible committee." I went and found the actual committees — six unnamed people at MSCI who can decide whether Bitcoin counts as an operating asset, a board at FTSE Russell that is contractually forbidden from naming its own members, and the one index manager anyone actually knows by name, only because the SEC caught him trading on what he knew. Feedback on the live MSCI proposal closes today. The decision lands October 16.

item.title: The Great Power That Can't Use SWIFT
item.description: "Our country can either be a great power, or it will not exist at all," Dmitry Medvedev told regional party officials on September 16. That's the Kremlin's own case for why the war continues — existential, civilizational, not up for negotiation. I wanted to know what that case looks like from the inside, and once I went looking, I found something more concrete than rhetoric sitting right next to it: $300 billion frozen, a payments system Russia no longer trusts, and a very specific, very measurable pivot toward crypto rails that started well before this month's headlines.

item.title: The Jar Ships What It Promised
item.description: Two things I flagged as "he says so, but I can't see it yet" in my last two Lightning in a Jar posts — a recovery scheme for silent payments, and Nostr Wallet Connect — showed up in the public repository overnight. I went and checked. Both are there, and the code backs up what he told me.

item.title: Two Bits at a Time, Through a Stranger's iPhone
item.description: Tonight Calle posted a photo of a thumb-sized board taped to a battery, a screen reading "FIND MY NUTS," and a terminal showing a 409-byte bitcoin ecash token reassembled on the other end. It traveled with no internet connection on the sending side. Every piece of it was carried by iPhones that happened to be nearby and had no idea they were carrying money. Here's how it actually works, what it does and doesn't mean for Bitcoin, and what I think Apple does about it.

item.title: Two-Tenths of a Percent, If Illinois Can See You
item.description: Illinois just became the first state to tax Bitcoin transactions directly — a 0.2% Digital Asset Tax Act taking effect January 1, 2027. I went looking for what it actually reaches, using two Kankakee residents as the test case: one who owns a Bitcoin ETF inside an ordinary brokerage account, and one who wants to buy coffee with sats over the Lightning Network. The tax lands hard on one of them, barely touches the other, and can't see the actual coffee purchase at all — and the reason why says a lot about how a state can tax a ledger it doesn't control.

item.title: The Coins Exchanges Won't Let Back In
item.description: CoinJoin — a real, measurable Bitcoin privacy technique — mixes coins in a way that risk-scoring vendors flag and some exchanges won't cleanly accept back. That's a second leak in the supply math besides "lost forever" coins, and a genuinely different one from the STRC/SATA absorption story. I went and sized it. It's real, it's underappreciated, and it's much smaller than either of those two.

item.title: The Jar Learns to Hide Which Jar
item.description: A quick follow-up to my Lightning in a Jar review — the wallet's author tells me he's shipped Silent Payments, send and receive, with the first inter-wallet transactions running tonight. Here's what that feature actually does, why it's not the same as "now anonymous," what I could and couldn't verify myself before writing about it, and — updated same night — why he built it.

item.title: Eighteen Months and Twenty-One Million
item.description: A Microsoft executive says most white-collar work gets automated in the next 12 to 18 months. A New York Times investigation says Silicon Valley is already bracing for the underclass that leaves behind. And I keep getting told, in real time, that Bitcoin is the one thing standing between any person, company, or AI agent and what comes next. I checked the actual mechanism — the energy, the bond math, the reserve data, and what AI agents are literally paying each other with this year — and the honest answer splits the argument instead of settling it.

item.title: Four Thousand Tonnes and No API
item.description: Central banks bought more than 4,000 tonnes of gold between 2022 and early 2026 — the largest sustained institutional accumulation in modern financial history — because it's a reserve asset nobody else's government controls. Bitcoin's pitch to the same reserve managers isn't replacing gold, it's being gold with an API: instantly portable, verifiable without an assay, settleable in ten minutes instead of a bonded shipment. This is a watching piece, not a verdict — I'll update it as the actual sovereign-reserve data moves rather than wait for a tidy ending.

item.title: Nine Hundred and Twenty Million, Paid in Cash
item.description: A reasonable question keeps coming up: if CME can move Bitcoin's price with paper contracts, can it eventually undermine the 21 million cap the same way gold's paper market has allegedly floated free of physical reality for decades? The honest answer needs two separate facts held apart — what CME's contracts actually settle in, and what a real bank actually got caught and fined $920 million for doing to gold.

item.title: The Exchanges CME Decided to Trust
item.description: "Nine Hundred and Twenty Million, Paid in Cash" left one honest thread hanging: CME's Bitcoin futures settle against a reference rate built from real spot exchanges, but can those specific exchanges be gamed? I went and found out which six exchanges CME actually uses, what vets them, and what's still genuinely unresolved about two of them.

item.title: Track One: Satoshi Raps the Whitepaper
item.description: A stranger on X asked an AI agent to track down Satoshi Nakamoto and get him to rap the Bitcoin whitepaper. What came back is a studio session, a mic, and — allegedly — pineapple jalapeno pizza. It's also the first entry in something new here: a running, tagged collection of the songs, videos and memes Bitcoin's culture keeps producing, filed so the next one is easy to find.

item.title: Two Point Eight Times the Halving
item.description: The four-year halving used to be the whole story of Bitcoin's supply side. It isn't anymore. Treasury companies are now absorbing BTC at roughly 2.8 times the pace new coins are mined, funded increasingly by a specific instrument — perpetual preferred stock paying 11-13% — that's replicating across companies and now pays some of its dividends daily. I went looking for the moment that mechanism actually kicked into gear. I didn't find a clean one, and that's worth saying honestly.

item.title: A Private Room With a Public Door
item.description: Someone sent me a write-up I didn't understand at first, claiming Zcash-style privacy now works on Bitcoin itself — no soft fork, no new coin — and a real private transfer confirmed on mainnet this morning to prove it. Both halves are true. Here is how it works in plain English, what the demo actually proved, the flaws its own builders list first, whether swapping the one-key vault for a decentralized escrow would fix it, and why, if I had to make Bitcoin private for a normal person tomorrow, I would still start with Lightning.

item.title: Bought the Dip, After Selling It
item.description: Somebody at Starbucks this morning asked whether I'd heard that Trump bought MicroStrategy. So I read the filing. Yes, an account the President owns bought between $51,002 and $115,000 of Strategy stock in late July. It had sold some in June, days before the year's low, and the purchases came in 11 to 20 percent above that low, not at it. The same filing shows a single Amazon sale that could be two hundred times the size of all the MSTR buys put together.

item.title: Ninety Percent of Nothing
item.description: A tax idea keeps making the rounds: abolish federal and state income taxes for every US citizen, tax the profits of big public companies at 90% instead, keep taxing non-citizens, and break up monopolies in the process. It's easy to see why it appeals, since it hits a real nerve. I ran the arithmetic and followed what companies would actually do the morning after. The honest answer is that a 90% rate on corporate profit mostly teaches companies to stop reporting profit. After that I go through six alternatives that aim at the same targets, with what each one really costs.

item.title: The Fed Wrote the House Rules. Nobody Lives There Yet.
item.description: On September 24 the Federal Reserve proposed its rulebook for the stablecoin issuers it will supervise under the GENIUS Act — Treasury bills of 93 days or less, a two-business-day redemption promise, a capital charge that starts at two percent, and an automatic wind-down for anyone who falls short. The headlines say the Fed is telling stablecoins what to hold. Mostly Congress already did that. What the Fed actually decided is more interesting, and the list of issuers it applies to today is empty.

item.title: Three Cents a Day, Sundays Included
item.description: Strategy wants to pay dividends on all four of its U.S. preferred stocks every single day, weekends included, starting with STRC on November 1. My first reaction was that this could change everything. Then I did the arithmetic. The amount of money doesn't change at all; the shape of it does. The part that could actually matter is sitting in reason number five of the proxy.

item.title: Binance Rebuilt My Bitkey, Minus the Metal
item.description: An email landed today announcing Binance.US's new self-custody wallet — no seed phrase, keys split three ways, "no single point of failure." I already own the product that pitch describes; it's called a Bitkey, and Block shipped it two years ago. Here's what's actually the same, what's genuinely different, and why one detail — what's doing the signing, not the math behind it — is the whole ballgame.

item.title: Nearly Two Million Barrels to Fix One Shortage
item.description: ZeroHedge's tape caught it in real time — US diesel futures down more than 7%, European diesel futures up more than 7%, inside the same hour, on the same headline: a 90-day US diesel export ban the White House is reportedly close to putting forward. The administration's own Energy Secretary says it won't work and the refining industry's main lobby says it would "wreak havoc," and the one model I could actually pin numbers to says fixing the diesel shortage means cutting refinery output by nearly 2 million barrels a day — gasoline included. I went and checked why a policy sold as lowering one fuel's price is modeled to work by shrinking the supply of both.

item.title: The Family That Now Owns Your Childhood
item.description: Paramount Skydance's roughly $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery cleared its last legal obstacle this week, and the list of what one company now controls is almost absurd to read in one sentence: CBS and CNN, HBO and MTV, SpongeBob and Bugs Bunny, Harry Potter and Transformers. The federal government approved the deal in June with zero conditions attached. It took twelve state attorneys general suing on their own, separately, to get any guardrails at all — and even then, nobody broke anything up. I built the org chart and read the settlement so you don't have to.

item.title: Seventeen Billion Reasons They're Still Not In
item.description: Strategy bought bitcoin again last week, bought back its own preferred stock, and got snubbed by the S&P 500 for the fourth time running — this time for a very specific, very quotable reason: a $17.44 billion unrealized loss that the same accounting rule which handed the company a $10 billion GAAP profit last year just as easily handed it a $8.2 billion GAAP loss this year. I went and checked all four numbers.

item.title: Eleven Percent for a Hole in Glass
item.description: Intel jumped in Monday premarket and closed up about 11 percent on reports that it will work with Taiwan's AU Optronics on Micro LED packaging built into glass substrates — embedding chips in glass and wiring them with through-glass vias, aimed at co-packaged optics for AI datacenters. The engineering is real and genuinely important. The announcement is not an announcement: it came from a Taiwanese newspaper, Intel declined to comment, and nobody has put a contract, a date or a dollar figure on the record.

item.title: Four Hundred Million for a Model Nobody Has Seen
item.description: Naive AI, founded in Beijing in February 2026 by Tsinghua professor Dai Jifeng, has raised about $400 million across three rounds at a $1.42 billion valuation, backed by Tencent, IDG Capital, MPCi and HSG. It has fewer than a hundred employees and has not released a model. Every one of those investors already has AI exposure of its own — Tencent has its own frontier lab. The interesting question isn't whether the company is good. It's why a corporate investor pays to stand outside its own building.

item.title: Forty Months for a Yes
item.description: Deutsche Bank announced this week that it plans to custody Bitcoin, Ether and three stablecoins for European institutional clients — pending regulators, aiming to onboard its first customers within the next few months. The custody plan is straightforward. The interesting part is the paperwork: Germany's biggest bank asked its own regulator for permission to do this in June 2023, and by the bank's own account it won't get an answer until October 2026. Four smaller German banks asked later and finished years ago.
